zeno_description: Anonym. Drachme nach dem Vorbild der Gepräge des Hormizd IV. vor 655, Tiflis. Büste mit kombinierter Krone, im linken Feld christliches Kreuz / Feueraltar zwischen 2 Wächtern. Mitchiner, Oriental Coins 1330; Paruck Tf. XXVII, 22 (Bartholomaei Coll.). 3.94 g. Äusserst selten Sehr schön Die wenigen bekannten Exemplare dieses hochinteressanten Münztyps stammen samt und sonders aus dem Kaukasus-Gebiet. Sie stehen in enger Verbindung mit den von Mitchiner (a.a.O.) erwähnten Drachmen vom Typ des Hormizd IV., welche die Monogramme verschiedener christlicher Herrscher von Tiflis (Guaram I, Stefan I. und Stefan II.) in georgischer Schrift tragen. Terminus ante quem für all diese Gepräge ist das Jahr 655 (oder 35 AH), in welchem Tiflis von den Arabern erobert wurde.

name: KL yr. 21, Sasanian AR drachm, Khusru I
zeno_description: I have an attractive coin of Khusro I that I bought in the summer of 1994 at the Beyazidiye coin market in Istanbul. At the same time and from the same guy I bought a handful of the more common Khusro II types. I think I paid between $3.00 and $5.00 a coin. The Khusro II group are authentic. I am no expert and have no reference books for this series. Would someone be able to tell me if Khusro I, mint KR, 23 regnal year is a rare type or a known forgery. My coin weighs about 4.3g (on a well-worn high school chemistry balance). The coin has a uniform black-brown patina. I am not unduly worried about forgeries and I have to admit that forging Late-Sassanian silver coinage seems mostly silly. The reasons why I think this coin may be a forgery follow: 1. The figures, particularly on the obverse, have few sharp details. 2. The figures on both sides seem to sink into the field, producing a tiny trough and then a bulge. I would compare the appearance to lumps of dough pressed into an unbaked pie crust. One might be able to see this most clearly around the crescent to the right of Khusro’s crown. Are these features in any way typical of Sassanian coins prior to Khusro II, few of which I have examined in hand? 3. The fields themselves and the area outside the border are uneven and lumpy. 4. The patina is absolutely uniform, especially on the obverse, and extends even to the hard-to-reach places. 5. At about two o’clock on the edge sloping away from the obverse is a patch of abrasions. It is no more than 4 mm long. The abrasions all go the same way, are evenly spaced, and seem to be predate the patina. I discovered this while looking at the coin under a stereo microscope (once again borrowed from the science faculty).
